content: The treatment success rate for patients with extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) is only 39%. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis recommend the use of an all-oral shorter treatment regimen due to its favorable anticipated effects. Analysis of outcomes comparing shorter bedaquiline-containing regimens (9–12 months) with longer all-oral regimens showed comparable efficacy. The shorter regimen demonstrated advantages, particularly in reducing the rates of patients lost to follow-up. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) determined that the anticipated desirable effects of the shorter regimen were modest. They noted that when bedaquiline is included in both shorter and longer regimens, the outcomes between the two groups are not significantly different. However, the shorter regimen offers the benefit of reduced treatment duration and improved follow-up adherence. Regarding undesirable effects, the GDG highlighted that the increased use of bedaquiline has alleviated concerns about its potential adverse effects. The undesirable effects of shorter and longer regimens containing bedaquiline are not expected to differ significantly, though they may vary depending on factors such as patient selection, disease severity, drug resistance patterns, and quality of care. In December 2018, WHO emphasized prioritizing fully oral longer regimens for most patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), while injectable agents were no longer considered a priority. The overall certainty of evidence for the effects of shorter regimens was rated as very low due to reliance on observational data and potential residual confounding. Despite efforts to adjust for confounders, some bias likely remains. Patients and civil society representatives expressed preferences for treatment regimens with minimal side effects, even if the treatment duration was longer. Survivors of drug-resistant TB indicated a willingness to accept longer regimens with fewer severe side effects over shorter regimens with more serious adverse effects. Preferences were primarily guided by the severity of side effects and, secondarily, by treatment efficacy. The balance of effects between shorter and longer regimens likely favors the shorter regimen due to its reduced duration and lower rates of loss to follow-up. Cost analyses in South Africa projected savings of approximately $3,000 per patient with the shorter regimen, with savings varying across settings depending on healthcare and drug costs. The shorter regimen was found to be both cost-saving and effective in all modeled scenarios. The GDG noted that shorter, injection-free regimens would be easier to implement in remote and underserved areas, potentially reducing health inequities. The absence of injectable agents eliminates the need for daily injections, reducing pain and adverse events for patients. However, the implementation of shorter regimens requires robust laboratory infrastructure for drug susceptibility testing (DST) and monitoring of bedaquiline resistance. The GDG recommended a shorter, all-oral, bedaquiline-containing regimen of 9–12 months for eligible patients with confirmed MDR/RR-TB who have not been exposed to second-line TB medicines for more than one month and in whom fluoroquinolone resistance has been excluded. Subgroup considerations include the following: People living with HIV (PLHIV): The shorter regimen is expected to perform similarly in PLHIV, provided they are on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Children: The shorter regimen may be used in eligible children aged 6–17 years, taking into account specific requirements for companion drugs. Pregnant and lactating women: Due to the contraindication of ethionamide in pregnancy, an individualized, all-oral longer regimen is recommended for this group. Extrapulmonary TB: Clinical judgment should guide the use of the shorter regimen in patients with extensive or severe extrapulmonary TB. Active drug safety monitoring and management systems are essential to detect and address adverse events promptly. Research priorities include: Studies comparing shorter all-oral regimens containing bedaquiline and linezolid. Evaluations of shorter regimens in specific subgroups, such as pregnant women. Randomized controlled trials to increase the certainty of evidence for shorter regimens. Investigations into mechanisms of resistance to bedaquiline and genetic markers for resistance. Efforts to standardize data collection to inform global recommendations. In conclusion, the shorter, all-oral, bedaquiline-containing regimen offers significant advantages in terms of reduced treatment duration, cost savings, and improved adherence.
